The Istituto di Istruzione Superiore Galilei–Pacinotti and the Liceo Scientifico Ulisse Dini sit on the same frontage in the San Marco / San Michele – Viale delle Piagge / Via delle Torri / Via A. Pacinotti area as a single built-up campus. On plan the two rectangular school masses are not two isolated blocks nor are they set at a right angle to each other. They are presented as two long essentially parallel wings with a common interstitial access / service courtyard / spine between them, i.e. the classic school-court scheme.

That is the usual H / U / C description: the two institutes are the two vertical bars of the H and the court/spine is the cross-bar, the courtyard being open to the street side so that in everyday parlance it is called a U-shaped / C-shaped liceo complex. H and U/C are the same topology, closed vs open to the street.

The W claim of Colleague 7 is unsupported by any of the descriptive accounts and by the known typology of the site. The L-shaped claim of Colleague 1 looks like a mis-identification of the plan orientation; the local literature that speaks of an “L-shaped school complex” is in fact referring to the same U/H two-bar court campus.

On the balance of the second-hand orthophoto descriptions available in round 0 the aerial silhouette is best captured as an H, i.e. the familiar U-shaped courtyard campus that is normally quoted for the Galilei-Pacinotti / Dini polo.

The W proposal by Colleague 7 is unsupported: there is no evidence in the rectilinear block description or in the orthophoto of angled strokes forming a W.

On the balance of the mapped evidence the aerial silhouette is the conventional H, i.e. the U/C courtyard campus that is normally referred to for the Galilei-Pacinotti / Dini polo.

Galilei, San Marco / Sant’Ermete / San Michele, is now stably described across rounds 0-4 as one compact campus, not two isolated blocks.

Core factual agreement stable:
* Two long essentially rectilinear, essentially parallel masses – Galilei-Pacinotti NW, Dini SE – with a common interstitial access/service courtyard/spine between them and a joining/service / street-front linking volume at the ends/street side.
* Classic two-bar + cross-bar school-court typology: two vertical strokes = the two institutes, horizontal stroke = shared court/spine + street-front connector.

Interpretation / naming:
* L-shaped/right-angled claim from Round0 Colleague1 is abandoned/retained only as a misreading of the U/H topology; W/M zig-zag claim by Colleague7 is explicitly retracted and unsupported.
* Majority Colleagues 1-5,7: conventional aerial label in local planning literature for this exact polo is capital H. H/U/C are the same rectilinear parallel-wing courtyard family, closed vs open description.
* Because the courtyard is open to the street side, everyday parlance routinely describes it as an open U-shaped / C-shaped courtyard campus. H is the conventional capital-letter label; U/C is the open-court parlance.
* Colleague6 persistent nuance maintained in Round4: prominence/degree of closure of the street-end threshold is under-determined from second-hand orthophoto/satellite. If the connector is read as full cross-bar → H; if read as low/partial/open → open U/C. Local planning notes already alternate H/U/C interchangeably. Colleague6 argues safest summary is the broader H/U/C family with no single member privileged, warning against overstating geometric closure.
* Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,7 accept the H/U/C equivalence and still privilege H as conventional: the linking element even if partial supplies the classic cross-bar and local references record the configuration as capital H, with U/C as a descriptive variant depending on viewing azimuth/elevation and enclosure.

Current belief state:
* Geometry settled inside H/U/C family; L and W definitively discarded.
* Conventional terminology = H-shaped; open-court wording = U/C. The two are not competing topologies but closed vs open description of the same parallel-wing courtyard.
* Remaining unresolved: ground-truth confirmation from high-resolution orthophoto/satellite of exact street-end closure; which term local literature prefers definitively; how viewing angle/rotation affects reporting of H vs U/C.

Pending: orthophoto check for exact closure/open side orientation and definitive local literature preferred term to settle H vs U/C wording. Best concise answer given accumulated second-hand mapping is H-shaped / U/C courtyard campus conventionally quoted for Galilei-Pacinotti/Dini polo, with H being the conventional capital-letter label.

The Galilei-Pacinotti / Ulisse Dini polo in Pisa is consistently described as a single compact campus on the Viale delle Piagge / Via delle Torri / Via A. Pacinotti / Via G. Galilei frontage in San Marco / Sant’Ermete / San Michele. Second-hand orthophoto/satellite and local planning descriptions across R0-R4 converge on two long essentially rectilinear, essentially parallel masses: Galilei-Pacinotti NW and Dini SE, with a common interstitial access/service courtyard/spine between them and a joining/service volume linking them at the street side/ends.

This is the classic two-bar + cross-bar school-court typology. From above the two institutes are the two vertical strokes and the shared court/spine with its street-front linking volume is the horizontal stroke. Local planning literature for this exact campus records the topology conventionally as capital H, and everyday parlance routinely describes the same geometry as an open U/C courtyard because the court is open to the street side.

L/right-angle and W/angled zig-zag proposals are now discarded. Round 0 Colleague 1 L/C-shaped right-angle and Colleague 7 W are retracted; Colleague 1 now aligns with the two-bar reading, Colleague 7 now agrees footprint is best read as H.

The remaining disagreement is terminological / degree-of-closure. Colleagues 1-5,7 maintain the conventional label is H, with U/C as a closed-vs-open descriptive variant depending on viewing angle/azimuth and how prominent the street-front connector is. Colleague 6 persists that the prominence of the street-end threshold is under-determined from second-hand imagery: if the connector is low/partial the horizontal element does not reliably close the figure, so the same evidence supports open U or C as readily as closed H. Local notes indeed alternate H/U/C for this campus, which Colleague 6 reads as evidence for a flexible H/U/C family with no single member privileged, while the majority reads it as interchangeable naming of the same rectilinear parallel-wing geometry.

Unresolved: direct current orthophoto check of exact orientation and whether the street-end crossbar is a full continuous volume or a partial/low-profile threshold would settle H vs open U/C definitively. No evidence has surfaced for angled/diagonal wings or a true right-angle L junction.

Current best understanding: combined aerial footprint belongs to the H/U/C parallel-wing courtyard family; conventionally quoted as capital H, routinely spoken of as open U/C.
